title: Christian Conservatives Want Our Kids to Love Reading. I Do Too. https://slate.com/life/2026/11/classic-learning-test-education-conservative-christian-charter-school.html
author: Rebecca Onion
summary: Slate writer Rebecca Onion, a public-school believer who admits to wishing she could consider a classical school for her daughter, examines the rise of classical education and the Classic Learning Test. She is drawn by screen-free classrooms, small classes and household-name canon authors, but wary of a movement she sees as conservative and Christian and of siphoning public money. She takes two practice CLTs and does well on the verbal and grammar sections without studying, then learns from researchers that the test rewards familiarity with unexplained proper nouns and older texts, which its founder Jeremy Tate calls "fluency". She finds common ground and then loses it in conversation with Tate, who pairs admiration for St. John's College with online politics she dislikes. She ends with her friends starting a classics book club and asking who will start a classical-education movement for liberals, or better yet for everyone.
points: Anxiety among public-school parents about kids reaching college without reading whole books is feeding interest in classical education.
The CLT's verbal sections favour test-takers already familiar with older texts, which the founder calls "fluency" and critics call a validity problem.
Expansion of the test is tied to the political culture war and to school-choice funding that moves families toward classical schools.
Onion sees real appeal in screen-free classrooms, canon reading and small classes, but distrusts the surrounding politics and curriculum providers.
Her proposed answer is a classical revival that is not tied to one political or religious camp.
quotes: Take the flood of stories, some anecdotal and some backed by data, about kids getting all the way to college without learning how to read whole books. (Setting aside concerns of rigor, this is simply a missed opportunity. You only have one chance to meet Faulkner with a 16-year-old brain.)

It was this no-screens, A.I.-proof way of teaching, used at my own private high school, that set me on the path to hopeless lifetime humanities fandom. You can’t do it with a big class, or with students who didn’t do the reading.

For me, this claim turned out to be true: The verbal part of the CLT was fun. I shut off the rest of the internet, put on the Liz Phair I listened to in high school, and fell into some version of a humanities flow state.
In 2026 you started to be able to submit CLT scores when applying to elite service academies. (“The CLT is the gold standard,” Pete Hegseth wrote on X.)

Mark Sulzer, of the University of Cincinnati, explained that he had found that while the CLT’s verbal reasoning questions do require reading longer passages than those in the SAT, they generally require “a lower level of inference” from test takers.

Jeremy Tate, the founder of the Classic Learning Test and a passionate defender of its principles, described this quality of the test positively, as “fluency.” The CLT, he said, can assess whether you’ve “grappled with these older texts before and have the confidence that comes with having dealt with them.

I tried to work pretty hard to cultivate a bipartisan brand and perception” is how he put it. Often, Tate argues that classical education teaches people how to have better conversations, whatever “side” they’re on.
